content:
Since Chow Hang-tung has been imprisoned, her comrade Lau Ka-yi has dreamt of her many times. In those dreams, Chow Hang-tung and Lee Cheuk-yan somehow always leave prison, then immediately ask her to help prepare press conferences, protests, and even swim together to escape, holding a press conference while eating hotpot at the same time. "I can't take it anymore. I told her, could you please stop entering my dreams," she said with a wry smile. She also can't understand why, in the dreams, they can't just rest, properly enjoy hotpot or go hiking — "it's always one disaster after another." But that is probably what the bond called "comrades" is about. The two had discussed imprisonment many times before, so Chow's incarceration was within their expectations. But when actually facing it, thinking about the freedom-loving, cheerful Chow Hang-tung locked in a small cell, only able to see the outside scenery through barbed wire, Lau Ka-yi couldn't help but feel emotional. "If she feels something must be done and is worth doing, then let's do it together," Lau Ka-yi said. Comrades stick together through thick and thin. Everyone has their own post, and the primary duty of those who remain is to keep company. Even though Chow Hang-tung has become a "high-risk figure," she would absolutely not deny her as a friend because of that: "We must live well and walk this road together to the end — at least until all our friends graduate out of here."

In early 2014, Chow Hang-tung, Lau Ka-yi, Lee Cheuk-yan and others shaved their heads to show support for Liu Xia. (Photo provided by interviewee)

Sixteen years of friendship — witnessing the shy "little sister" grow up

Lau Ka-yi, a member of the "Tiananmen Mothers Movement" and former standing committee member of the Hong Kong Alliance in Support of Patriotic Democratic Movements of China, is a regular observer of the case. She met Chow Hang-tung after 2010, when Chow returned to Hong Kong from the University of Cambridge to work as a staff member of the Alliance. Having already heard that Chow had organised June Fourth anniversary events in the UK, she recalled their first meeting, finding Chow rather shy, often giggling, and "not saying much," but whenever topics like conditions in China or human rights and social movements came up, her eyes would light up as she listened.

She said Chow Hang-tung came from an elite school background, but never confined herself to a particular role or thought she was someone special — moving things around, distributing flyers, running street booths and shouting through megaphones, pushing donation boxes — "wherever people are needed, she fills in." Within her abilities, she was willing to do anything and give her all. At that time, the social movement circle faced a severe lack of fresh blood. Watching Chow Hang-tung absorb and progress like a sponge, Lau Ka-yi felt she was "a talent worth keeping."

After about half a year with the Alliance, Chow moved to an NGO focusing on mainland China's labour rights. To better safeguard grassroots interests and push the movement forward, a year later she began studying law. In 2014, she ran for the Alliance's standing committee, entering the legal profession, and the following year was elected vice-chairperson. Lau Ka-yi felt that over those years, Chow had gained more knowledge of mainland society, become more down-to-earth, and gradually developed her own working style. Her early ideals and passion had not been worn away, but she had begun to understand how difficult the situation was, and shared more of her thoughts. Facing localists' criticism that the Alliance was full of "Greater China apologists" and going through the motions, she was willing to try to understand and exchange views, and brought back stories of different mainland democracy activists to the Alliance.

Although the two had an age gap of more than ten years, they shared similar values, with no generational divide. Late-night hotpot, drinking and chatting, going hiking and travelling together were common occurrences. In Lau Ka-yi's eyes, Chow Hang-tung was unpretentious, frank and naive. Beyond the serious issues of democracy and human rights, in daily life she was utterly "goofy" — Lau recalled that once, not wanting to light the stove, she soaked instant noodles in hot water, then complained afterwards that it "tasted terrible"; another time, working late into the night at a law firm, she got hungry and couldn't find food, so she ate tea leaves. "Noodles are supposed to be cooked, for goodness' sake — who just dunks them till they're dead?" Lau Ka-yi still finds it absurd when she recalls it. "When it comes to everyday life things, she's really quite silly."

Early in her imprisonment, Chow Hang-tung once sent Lau Ka-yi a card with a kapok tree drawn on it. The kapok tree is also known as the "hero tree." Lau Ka-yi said Chow Hang-tung liked it very much, because she felt there were many unsung heroes in the democratic movement.

Seeing the outside world through "holes"

In 2021, Chow Hang-tung was imprisoned on multiple charges — not unexpected to Lau Ka-yi, who had long discussed imprisonment with her. She didn't cry because of Chow's arrest, but once, while watching a documentary about dissident Lin Zhao — who was executed during the Cultural Revolution and wrote blood letters in prison — she couldn't help but put herself in Chow's shoes and silently shed tears. It was early in Chow's sentence then, and whether situations like those on the mainland might emerge was still unknown. Watching Lin Zhao insist she had done nothing wrong and wanted to keep speaking out, Lau felt as if she were seeing Chow's shadow — those "foolish acts" in the eyes of the world: "I feel she really would do it."

Also in the early days of imprisonment, Chow Hang-tung sent a card to Lau Ka-yi with a kapok tree drawn on it, and rows of holes pierced on the other side. Chow carefully explained how to look at the card — those outside the wall see the kapok tree without holes, while she inside has to peer through the barbed wire, "seeing the outside world through so many holes," or else "face a wall with nothing there." Hearing this, Lau Ka-yi was deeply moved, and felt a bit heavy-hearted.

The card with rows of holes pierced into it represents her, inside the wall — having to peer through the barbed wire, "seeing the outside world through so many holes."

Companionship — the duty of those who remain

In the past, whether working, eating, drinking or having fun, the other was always there. Now, even doing the same things, "there's just one person missing." Every time after finishing a prison visit, walking alone back to the bus stop, Lau Ka-yi would feel deeply emotional: "She really is a cheerful, lively person... and now she's actually locked up. You have a person who loves freedom so much, with no freedom — but we can walk right out." Even if the scenery along the way is beautiful, "she can't see any of it now at all."

When missing Chow Hang-tung, Lau Ka-yi does things she likes, like hotpot or hiking. A group of friends once tried hiking up Tai Lam, gazing towards the prison where she is — "it felt like we'd accomplished something." Coming across good food or interesting places, she'd make a note of them, saving them to share with her in the future. Even the route from the prison, a group of friends deliberately explored the scenery nearby, hoping that when Chow Hang-tung is released they could slowly take her around to see the sights.

Lau Ka-yi feels everyone has their own post, and for those who remain, the primary responsibility now is companionship. To her, the road since 2019 isn't finished yet — "indeed there are still many people inside." Whether inside or outside the wall, walking this road together is also important. Companionship goes both ways. Lau Ka-yi feels that at every hearing, "she [Chow Hang-tung] is insisting on something, and that insistence is also accompanying Hong Kong's people."

Every time after finishing a prison visit and walking back to the bus stop, Lau Ka-yi feels deeply emotional: "She's really locked up now... but we can walk right out." The scenery along the way is beyond Chow Hang-tung's reach — "it's two completely different worlds."

Chow Hang-tung and Lee Cheuk-yan often appear in dreams

Since Chow Hang-tung was imprisoned, Lau Ka-yi has dreamed of her once every two weeks, and sometimes of Lee Cheuk-yan too. The dreams blend reality and fantasy — they always start with the two somehow leaving prison, astonishing her: "Huh? You're out again? Aren't you supposed to be inside?" Then they'd make strange requests — once, the two wanted to hold a press conference and told her to issue a press release. When reporters arrived, Chow Hang-tung somehow produced a stove from nowhere, saying they could hold a press conference while eating hotpot. Afterwards, the two dragged her swimming to Taiwan, and the moment they arrived, they immediately held a press conference and ate hotpot again.

"I said, since you're out, can you at least take a breather before holding a press conference? Then Ah Tung said she couldn't rest," Lau Ka-yi said with a laugh. "It's really exhausting... I don't understand why we can't just properly enjoy hotpot, or properly go hiking — it's always one disaster after another."

Another time, she dreamed of preparing a June Fourth march with former Alliance standing committee member Kwan Chun-pong. Suddenly Chow Hang-tung and Lee Cheuk-yan appeared, being chased. Kwan Chun-pong grabbed both of them and jumped into the sea — "Then Ah Bong sacrificed himself, he didn't float back up," Lau Ka-yi laughed heartily. "The two said, forget it, let's go!"

Lau Ka-yi said Chow Hang-tung and Lee Cheuk-yan often appear in her dreams. Once, Kwan Chun-pong (right three) grabbed both of them and jumped into the sea. She laughed and said, "Then Ah Bong was sacrificed."

Willingly playing the fool together

The subconscious is the most truthful — even though she appears very optimistic on the surface, when it comes to her good friend's imprisonment and loss of freedom, she can't help but feel worried and sad inside. And protests, press conferences — those are things this group of comrades used to do together. "In those dreams, you can feel that they have always been comrades."

So-called "comrades" are probably about "sharing the pot and sticking together through difficulties." Even things that seem silly, doing them with them is enjoyable and done willingly — "Even playing the fool, we play the fool together." She recalled that in 2014, when they shaved their heads to support Liu Xia, Chow Hang-tung was the first to raise her hand, and she followed suit: "Sigh, if you're going to shave, I'll shave too." In 2014, the two also tried posting "umbrella peddlers" with memo paper on a minibus, showing support for mainlanders arrested over the Umbrella Movement. "We didn't even know if it would have any effect... let's try first, if it doesn't work we'll think again."

From a friend's perspective, she certainly feels that Chow Hang-tung is suffering in prison, and wants her to "come out soon and take a breather." But from a comrade's perspective, she sees the whole democratic movement, and "sacrificing the small self for the greater good" is Chow's choice. Friend and comrade coexist. Lau Ka-yi gave a light-hearted example — normally she'd remind Chow Hang-tung to take care of her health, but she also says without fail: "If you die in prison, we'll definitely make a big deal of it for you." "Honestly, even if we didn't say anything, she would definitely keep doing what she does."

Around 2018, Chow Hang-tung hand-made two leather coin purses and gave one to Lau Ka-yi, saying "it's the first thing she's ever handmade." Lau Ka-yi thinks it's quite pretty, and occasionally uses it, joking: "It's rare for her to give something, the first time she's given me anything in all the years we've known each other."

Only with freedom is there possibility

Arrested in 2024 on a sedition charge under Article 23, Lau Ka-yi frankly admits that with untouchable red lines, she has become more cautious in what she says and does. But she states clearly: "I won't, just because you've arrested me, deny Chow Hang-tung as my friend. I won't do that... this is really the absolute bottom line."

Before Chow Hang-tung went to prison, Lau Ka-yi once asked her: if one day she was behind bars, would she want Lau to fly far away and speak freely, or to stay but be unable to say anything? Chow immediately said, "Of course stay — at least keep me company chatting."

"Well, I've done it. I stayed to chat with her," Lau Ka-yi smiled. After the verdict, she expects to return to Taiwan to finish her studies, but says she won't disappear, and will continue writing and visiting. She said Chow Hang-tung actually wants people to "chat more" with her.

Chow Hang-tung, who loves debating with friends, once wrote to Lau Ka-yi saying that in prison no one would "argue" with her — people only praised her and cheered her on, making her soul feel like it was dying and drying up. "So I just wrote back a letter to scold her," Lau Ka-yi said.

Having known each other for many years, expressing mutual companionship and waiting would be too mushy: "So cheesy, I'd want to throw up after saying it... let's just understand without saying anything," she said in exasperation. Is there anything she wants to say to Chow Hang-tung? "Come out soon for hotpot — you owe me that many meals," she said in her usual half-joking tone, before adding seriously: "I also want you to have freedom soon — only with freedom is there any other possibility."

The two used to love hotpot most. Asked what she wants to say to Chow Hang-tung, Lau Ka-yi immediately joked: "Come out soon for hotpot — you owe me so many meals!" (Photo provided by interviewee)

Disappointed by the verdict: will lay out the truth in the sunlight

On 21 August 2026, Chow Hang-tung was convicted of inciting subversion of state power. Outside the court, Lau Ka-yi, wearing a yellow raincoat and a "The People Will Not Forget" T-shirt, first escorted Chow Hang-tung's mother away, then told reporters that as a friend and former Alliance standing committee member, she was disappointed by the verdict: "We have always hoped to pursue democracy, we have always sincerely mourned the June Fourth victims and cared for the mothers of Tiananmen." Her tone was firm.

"For June Fourth, no crime. For mourning, no crime. We will continue to walk the path through the courts, continue through the appeal process to make the truth, to make what we understand, clear, laid out under the sun's view, so the public can see clearly what the arguments are. Justice is in people's hearts."

Lau Ka-yi said that regarding the Alliance sedition case, Chow Hang-tung will definitely appeal all the way to the Court of Final Appeal.
